Thank you. Good morning and welcome to a meeting of the Subcommittee on Zoning and Franchises. I am Council Member Farrah Louis, Chair of the Subcommittee. This meeting is being held remotely via Zoom. Pursuant to the Emergency Declaration signed by Governor Hochul on February 21st, 2026, Executive Order 58, the council has determined that this— that the winter storm has impaired the council's ability to hold in-person meetings and that all council meetings today are being conducted remotely via Zoom. Thank you in advance for your patience this morning. This morning, I am joined remotely by council members - give me one second. Salaam, Sanchez, Ossé, Encarnación, Thomas-Henry. If I'm missing anyone else, please let me know.
Chair, I see Council Member Carr is present.

Thank you and Council Member Carr. Today we are only voting on three proposals and there is no public hearing. As a result, public testimony will not be heard today. Members of the public are able to view this meeting via the council's website at www.council.nyc.gov. Scroll down to the meeting information for today’s date and click See More Details. From there, a public link for video access will be available. Before I go over today's votes, I recognize the Committee Counsel to go over the meeting's procedures.

Thank you, Chair Louis. I am, uh, Arthur Ha, counsel to this Subcommittee. Council members, uh, who would like to ask questions or make remarks should use the Zoom raise hand function. The raise hand function, uh, should appear at the bottom of your screen. Council members with remarks or questions will be, um, uh, will be called in the order in which their hands are raised, uh, and recognized by the Chair. We ask everyone that you please be patient if any technical difficulties arise today.

Uh, Chair Louis, we are going to, uh, I believe we're going to stand at ease for one second, but I will, um, I will text you in the chat. Um, once we resume, Chair, uh, the Chair will continue with today's agenda.
Thank you. I just wanna repeat for the record, the Subcommittee will stand at ease for a few moments, and we've also been joined by Council Member Farias.
I'm here, Farah, if you need my vote.
Okay, right now we're at ease. Give us a few minutes.
Okay, I'm doing it on my phone so that I can leave on the BNT meeting on my computer.
All right, as soon as we're ready to vote, I'll text you.
I can stay on, I'm on already, so—
Chair, I'm on as well.
Got it. Thank you. Okay, we will now resume. Arthur?
Thank you, Chair. Uh, we can proceed with the agenda. You can, um, resume, uh, on the remarks from 24th Avenue.

Got it. Thank you. The first proposal concerns LUs 20 and 21 related to 217-14 24th Avenue. Rezoning project in Council Member Paladino's district. Applicant is seeking to develop a mixed-use residential project with approximately 183 apartments and 65 long-term care living units in Bay Terrace, Queens. The proposal involves two actions. The first is a Zoning Map Amendment to change the existing residential R1-2 district to a residential R6A district. The second action is a Zoning Text Amendment to map a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area. Council Member Paladino supports this application. Is Council Member Paladino on? I don't see her.
I know, Chair, I do not see, uh, Council Member Paladino here.

Thank you so much, Arthur. The second proposal concerns LUs 33 and 34 related to 33-01 11th Street rezoning project in Council Member Cabán's district. Applicant is seeking to develop a

mixed-use residential project with approximately 258 apartments in Ravenswood, Queens. The proposal involves two actions. The first is a Zoning Map Amendment to change the existing residential R-5 district to a residential R-7A paired with a manufacturing M-1-4 district. The second action is a Zoning Text Amendment to map a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area. We are recommending one modification to remove MIH Option 2 and add Option 3, which will ensure that the affordable housing to be— the affordable housing to be provided is actually affordable to the residents in this part of the city. Council Member Cabán supports this application with, with the recommended modification. The third proposal concerns LU-28 and 29 related— the third proposal concerns LU-28 and 29 related to 14-10 Beach Channel Drive rezoning project and Council Member Brooks-Powers' district. Applicant is seeking to develop a mixed-use residential project with approximately— that will include permanent— permanently affordable apartments in Far Rockaway, Queens.

The proposal involves 2 actions. The first, a Zoning Map Amendment to change the existing residential R-5 district to a residential R-6A district with a commercial C2-4 overlay. The second action is a Zoning Text Amendment to map a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area. We are recommending a modification to the rezoning area and proposed Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area. A proposed and rezoning area includes both applicant, applicant site, which primarily consists of surface parking and several existing homes. The modification is to reduce the rezoning area to the applicant site. This will ensure that the residents of the existing houses are not pressured into moving so that their homes can be— so that their homes can be torn down to build apartments, which they will not be able to afford. Displacement pressure in low-income Black and brown communities due to upzoning is real. Constituents in Council Member Brooks-Powers' district regularly contact her office about being pressured to sell by developers. Residents in downtown Far Rockaway are facing the same risks, and this issue cannot continue to go unaddressed.

To reflect this change in the rezoning area, the Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area to be applied through the proposed tax amendment should be limited to the development site. I know Council Member Brooks-Powers is on. Would you like to make remarks?

Thank you again, Chair, and thank you to the— my colleagues on the Subcommittee. The proposal before us for 14-10 Beach Channel Drive is the result of real negotiation. Um, from the beginning, my focus has been simple. We must deliver meaningful benefits for the Rockaway community. The project before us today looks very different from where it started, thanks in large part to community input. Studio apartments have been removed, and the building now includes a stronger concentration of 2 and 3-bedroom units—housing that actually works for families. The parking has also been increased to a 1-to-1 ratio, which reflects the transportation realities of the peninsula. The applicant has committed to continuing to pursue affordable homeownership options, which is critical. Our community needs ownership pathways that

allow working families to build equity. There are additional commitments that matter, including air quality monitoring during nearby industrial operations with filtration systems installed if necessary, a 30% MBE and local hiring goal, including outreach within Community Board 14, apprenticeship and job training programs during the project's construction, funding support for improvements at the Child Center for New York operating at Redburn Housing— Houses. A signed MOU giving Glory Light Tabernacle a right of first refusal for a below-market community facility space set at 60% of the market rate value. This is not unconditional support. It is the support based on commitments secured through engagement. With those commitments on record. I will be voting yes. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member Brooks Powers. Counsel, are there any council members with questions or remarks at this time?

Any other Subcommittee members or any other council members, uh, wishing to make remarks or ask questions should now please use the raise hand function, and especially if you are not

named as a Committee Member or Council Member, please, uh, do use the raise hand function now uh, if you wanna make comments or ask questions. Chair, I am not seeing any hands raised.

Thank you so much. I now call for a vote to approve with modifications LU-33 and 34 related to 33-01, 11th Street Rezoning Proposal. LU-28 and 29 related to 14-10 Beach Channel Drive Rezoning Proposal. LUs 20 and 21 related to the 217-14 24th Avenue Rezoning Proposal. Counsel, please call the roll.
Chair, if I may, just to, uh, clarify that the vote for LUs 20 and 21 is to approve. Uh, and with that-
Yes.

Aye on all.

I vote aye on all.
Council Member Schulman?
Aye, aye on all.
Thank you.

I vote aye on all.

Yes!

Council Member Justin Sanchez?
I vote aye on all. Thank you.
Council Member Thomas-Henry?
Aye on all.
Minority Leader, uh, Carr.
Aye on all.

Thank you, Counsel. That concludes today's business. I would like to thank the members of the public, my colleagues, Subcommittee

Counsel, land use, and other council staff, and the Sergeant-at-Arms for participating in today's meeting. This meeting is hereby adjourned. Thank you.
Good job, gentlemen.
Zoom is now ending.
Thank you.

Thank you, everyone.

Counsel, are there any Council Members who have raised their hands to make a comment on this application? COMMITTEE COUNSEL: Council members wishing to make remarks or ask questions should use the Zoom raise hand function. Chair, I don’t see anyone with the hand raised at the moment. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Okay, uh, we will also vote, ah, to approve LUs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 for the Constellation HPD project, which is a set of

applications by HPD seeking the designation of an Urban Development Action Area, Urban Development Action Area project, and the disposition of public land— of city-owned land together with an Article 11 tax exemption to enable the development of a cluster of 8 new buildings containing income-restricted affordable housing, own— homeownership units in the Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brownsville, East Flatbush, and East New York, in Council Members Bank and Mealy’s district. Counsel, are there any Council Members who have raised their hands to make a comment on this application? COMMITTEE COUNSEL: Checking now, Chair. No, I don't see any members with the raised hand at the moment. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: I see Council Member Mealy. COUNCIL MEMBER MEALY: Yes, thank you, Chair, and thank you for this opportunity to at least let you know what's going on with these, um, these projects. I definitely love affordable housing, but now to find out that it's only co-ops, and I feel we are doing this city an injustice if we let, um, this development go through in regards to— we've given

them the land for 99 years, we've given them a 40-year tax abatement, and then we definitely, um, Community Land Trust will own the property for 99 years, and here it is, the AMI is totally too high for Brownsville. You can't wipe this clean slate, everyone has the same income bracket, and I asked HPD to try to at least have it more affordable for my constituents in Brownsville, in which this may be their last opportunity to have affordable homeownership. So if they could have at least put down the AMI lower that this American dream could come true to lease the tax bracket in Brownsville would be much appreciated. But if they cannot do that, I'm not, 'cause I will not be voting on this going forward, 'cause I feel this is the last opportunity. You could say that it's affordable, but affordable to who? We've been saying this over and over and over. This is an opportunity for HPD and this body to give true homeownership, and I'm just asking my colleagues— they could say talk later, but after the, the horse then went out the gate after that, they could say 80% AMI after we vote for this.

So I know it's a time restraint, but I can't consciously, because I know this will be the end of my Brownsville district with really owning the American dream with homeownership. So I just hope that my colleagues could consider abstaining, at least that if HPD say that they willing to work with me, let's see if they do. But just to give them a blanket yes right now and say later I talk to you, I'm, I'm not confident, confident in that it will be done, and I just hope you could give me this opportunity. Thank you, Chair, and thank you for at least listening and calling to find out how things are going, and I appreciate that, and I hope my colleagues understand I wanna be the team player. In my whole gut, I know what this project could mean, but I know I can't sacrifice homeownership for, um, whole section of my district. It's, it's supposed to be for the whole city. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Uh, Council Member Banks. COUNCIL MEMBER BANKS: Ah, good morning everyone. Um, hold on, let me just make sure I have my— one minute. Uh, just a follow-up. I thought all concerns and questions were addressed pertaining to the, uh, 8

constellations, um, and the concerns that, uh, Council Member Mealy had put forth. I, I thought that they were addressed already. Um, I've— I'm, I'm actually satisfied with the 2 that are slated for my particular Councilmatic District. Um, and, uh, we are, uh, you know, we, we believe that these particular, uh, these two projects that in our district will lead to homeownership, um, and these constellation projects, uh, these are the, the, the type of development, uh, that my community is, uh, is proud to see moving forward. Um, this initiative will create new pathways to affordable homeownership, uh, paired with thoughtful, uh, sustainable design. Uh, these projects also, uh, the, the, um, they just don't add housing. Uh, it creates an opportunity that gives working families a chance to put their roots down, build equity, and remain in neighborhoods they've helped shape for generations. So I was proud to support the— this effort. We also, uh, supported it, were given $100,000 in capital funding, uh, because we wanted to, you know, believe in expanding access to homeownership has been and is the priority, um, one of the things I've ran on as a Council Member. Um, so these council— this Constellation

project represents real progress for the 42nd Council District. And I remain committed, uh, to advancing this development, um, that centers, centers residents and strengthens communities and expands the true affordability across the city. Um, I'm hoping that, uh, the concerns that are being put forth by, um, my good, good different colleague Council Member Mealy, hopefully we can get those addressed. But, uh, as far as, uh, Um, my concern as a Council Member for the 42nd, the 2 that are in my district, uh, we are in fully support. So we ask that the, uh, once the concerns are addressed from Council Member Mealy, that we move forward with, with a vote. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Uh, Council Member Thomas-Henry. COUNCIL MEMBER THOMAS-HENRY: Thank you, Chair. So my question was, since Council Member Mealy does have an issue with the ones that are in her district, do all— does this have to be coupled, or could we vote on them separately? CHAIRPERSON MARTE: So the way I understand it is that, um, it has to be coupled. Uh, it's a, it's a multi-development application, and that's how it was

presented to us by HPD. And from my understanding, there's still ongoing negotiation. Is there any way Um, do we know how soon that will be wrapped up or put in writing? Um, so the last that I heard was that, uh, HPD is putting something on paper, um, to continue discussion post-ULRP to explore ways to potentially target lower AMIs of 50% at 8587 Legion Street. 14 homeownership units and 250-254 Hertz Street, which is 14 home— homeownership units, and we'll follow up with my office and Mealy's office about, uh, doing so before closing. COUNCIL MEMBER THOMAS-HENRY: Thank you. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Any other— Council Members. COUNCIL MEMBER BANKS: Uh, Mr. Chair, if I may interject, uh, I was, uh, informed also— well, as, as I was also informed that there has been a, a commitment by HPD, uh, to, uh, to meet with the Council Member to address the AMI concerns, um, and that the, uh, the, the commitment, uh, was sent to the, the Council Member. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Thank you, Council Member Banks. Uh, Council Member Mealy— oh, you put your hands down.

COUNCIL MEMBER MEALY: No, I was still— did HPD say they wouldn't be able to pull that separate? So it's either do it or don't? CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Exactly, it's all, all one application. COUNCIL MEMBER MEALY: Well, I know it has been done before that they pulled it. I came from Florida one time and they split it and made sure that a church got a piece of the— piece, um, of the property that we was voting on. So are you sure they say they couldn't pull it out, or those two parcels? CHAIRPERSON MARTE: From, from my understanding. COUNCIL MEMBER MEALY: Please get clarity before, please, because I know what the HPD and developers can do. It's been done before. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: All right, give me one second to confirm this. I'll be right back. Uh, you cannot split the, the cluster, uh, because if you stop one project and it, you know, has consequences on the rest of the projects and they won't be built. Council Member Thomas Henry.

COUNCIL MEMBER THOMAS-HENRY: Apologies, one more question. Um, I know during the hearing I had asked if they, um, had looked at how long the maintenance for these plots, since they are co-ops, if there was some mechanism that was gonna be put in place to maintain a specific maintenance rate, um, for at least a certain period of time. So that, um, because that could down the line, um, really hinder the affordability of the units with increased maintenance costs skyrocket. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: I'm asking to see if we get an answer to that question, but I guess in the meantime uh, Councilmember Mealy, do you have another comment? So now to me, if someone get in, in a financial bind, they should be able to sell it to whoever they choose to, but no, it will have to go back to them. And then HPD said that they would give the homeowners a loan. I never heard of that before, but, um, this is so questionable that we don't want homeowners to get in a situation where they own it and then they can't attain it for the future down the line, and then if they lose it, who gets the property? It goes back to the community land trust. That's not an open market, and this is a— this is the community land trust will be the owners for 99 years. And it has to be some kind of— something that the homeowners can— if it do go up too high and they get in financial problems, what can they do? Could somebody from HPD explain that to let everyone get a full understanding what this project really is about? COUNCIL MEMBER BANKS: Mr. Chair? CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER BANKS: Yeah, from my knowledge, I don't think the property doesn't go back to the Community Land Trust. Uh, they can sell it and it

can— they, they can make profit on the sale if, if they get into any type of distress. Um, so I don't, I don't, I don't, I don't know if that's accurate. COUNCIL MEMBER MEALY: So we let land use explain the same thing they told me. I asked those questions intensively, and they still go back to the community land trust. So please let HPD explain it to you, because my district— you and my district is about the same, um, income level. So I'm making sure that my district would really be able to obtain these co-ops. This may be the last time, because everything else it's gonna be unattainable. So is HPD on that? They could explain it clearly to my colleagues. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: I don't— COUNCIL MEMBER HANIF: I just asked if what's happening right now is the right forum, because we, we all have other votes. CHAIRPERSON MARTE: Yeah, I, I, I, I, I agree, Council Member Hanif. COUNCIL MEMBER BANKS: Yeah, and, and, and Chair, just the last thing, just wanna also say this about the community land trust and the role that they'll play. Sanctuary City Policies are Critical for all New Yorkers

Immigrant New Yorkers are at significant risk of being separated from their families, communities, and jobs, and detained in jail-like conditions that cause rapid physical and mental health deterioration. Increasingly, people in immigration can be transferred anywhere in the country without the ability to seek a bond hearing. And it is now more likely that an ICE arrest and detention could result in deportation to a third country where a person has never been to, holds no status in, and could face dangerous or torturous conditions. Our neighbors are being snatched off the street by masked, plainclothes Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents or are being detained at the very courthouses they are visiting to abide by the legal process of the immigration system. The increase of federal agents in NYC not only creates fear in New Yorkers regardless of immigration status but also increases the likelihood of violent arrests and unlawful immigration detention. The city must take immediate steps to protect the rights of immigrant New Yorkers, expand immigration legal services, and ensure all New Yorkers know their rights.

Concerns highlighted in DOI Reports

The two recent Department of Investigation (DOI) reports that are the subject of this hearing highlight deeply concerning incidents in which New York City’s sanctuary laws were violated. The reports also warned there may be additional instances of local collusion with federal immigration authorities that were not detected, as well as broader systemic problems, including unclear agency policies, insufficient training of agency staff, and failures in tracking and documenting interactions with federal immigration authorities that create an ongoing risk of improper cooperation.

In September 2025, DOI issued a report DOI Investigation into DOC Correction Intelligence Bureau Investigator Assisting Federal Agents with Immigration Enforcement which found an employee of the Department of Correction (DOC) had violated the city sanctuary laws and DOC policy by sharing information on two people in DOC custody with federal civil immigration enforcement.

The second DOI report from December 2025, entitled DOI Investigation into the NYPD’s Compliance with Local Laws Restricting City Assistance with Immigration Enforcement1 highlighted a concerning incident in which an NYPD officer improperly assisted federal immigration enforcement by using NYPD resources. The December 2025 report warned there may be additional instances of local collusion with federal immigration authorities that were not detected. Beyond that single violation, this report highlights broader systemic problems— including unclear policies, insufficient training, and failures in tracking and documenting interactions with federal immigration authorities—that create an ongoing risk of improper cooperation.

The DOI reports should serve as a warning that city agencies are unable to uniformly comply with laws that have been in place for a decade and there is a clear need for increased guidance, training, and tightened data privacy.

This risk is particularly acute given the broader federal information-sharing systems already in place. Even where New York City limits direct cooperation with immigration enforcement, local law enforcement activity is already embedded in federal data systems. When a person is arrested, their fingerprints are automatically transmitted to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and, through interoperable databases, shared with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). This automatic data-sharing occurs nationwide and can trigger immigration enforcement, including home raids, the issuance of detainers, or the initiation of removal proceedings, regardless of how the underlying local case is ultimately resolved.2

In other words, routine contact with the criminal legal system—such as an arrest—can place individuals into the federal immigration enforcement pipeline, even in jurisdictions with strong sanctuary laws. In this context, any additional local data sharing, surveillance, or failure to comply with sanctuary protections compounds the risk and increases the likelihood that New Yorkers will be exposed to immigration enforcement.

These detainer discretion laws were intended to prevent non-citizens detained in DOC and NYPD custody from being transferred to immigration detention. However, given the intransigence of ICE’s aggressive apprehension and detention policies, and the agency’s enforcement priorities, years later, it is evident that our criminal legal system continues to cause non-citizens to be apprehended by ICE, as the vast majority of New York City residents detained by ICE have had contact with the criminal legal system. This needs to include the ability to enforce the law if or when it is not followed. Implement Executive Order 13 to Ensure Compliance with Sanctuary City Laws

Executive Order 13 is intended to ensure that New York City’s sanctuary laws are meaningfully implemented across all agencies by requiring clear guidance, training, and accountability when city employees interact with federal immigration authorities. However, the continued reporting of violations and the findings of oversight bodies make clear that these protections are not being consistently realized in practice.

A central concern is the persistent lack of understanding among city workers about what sanctuary laws require and what conduct is prohibited. Frontline staff are often placed in

situations involving federal immigration authorities without clear direction. This confusion is not incidental—it is the result of agencies failing to provide adequate guidance, training, and internal protocols to ensure compliance.

Our experience representing New Yorkers reflects these gaps in implementation. As described above, we have encountered repeated situations in which Department of Correction staff unlawfully refuse to release individuals after bail is paid based on the mistaken belief that the existence of an ICE detainer requires continued detention, even where the individual is clearly protected under the city’s detainer laws. Families are also frequently given incorrect information about the effect of ICE detainers. They are often told that bail cannot be posted, or that release will not occur, because of an “ICE hold.” As a matter of law, an ICE detainer alone does not provide a valid basis for continued detention once a person has met the conditions of release. This misinformation can deter families from posting bail, unnecessarily prolong detention, and increase the risk of immigration enforcement.

These implementation failures are compounded by deficiencies in oversight and reporting. City law requires agencies to document and report interactions with federal immigration authorities, including under the detainer laws, yet it remains unclear whether all agencies are consistently complying with these requirements. Incomplete or inconsistent reporting undermines transparency and limits the City Council’s ability to conduct meaningful oversight.

These concerns are further reinforced by public reporting. Media outlets, including Gothamist, Politico, the Associated Press, and The City, have documented multiple incidents in which city employees may have acted inconsistently with the city’s sanctuary laws. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that, despite the existence of Executive Order 13, gaps in implementation, training, and accountability persist across agencies.

Surveillance and Database Concerns

New York City’s sanctuary laws are intended to limit local involvement in federal immigration enforcement. However, the city’s extensive data collection and surveillance systems create parallel pathways through which sensitive information can be accessed, shared, or misused in ways that undermine those protections.

City agencies routinely collect and maintain large amounts of personal data through everyday operations, including benefits records, housing information through NYCHA, and law enforcement databases. At the same time, policing technologies—such as license plate readers, transit surveillance, and other monitoring tools—generate detailed records about New Yorkers’ movements, associations, and activities. These systems often contain inaccurate, incomplete, or unverified information, yet they can have significant consequences when accessed or relied upon by law enforcement or federal authorities.

When local agencies share sensitive information about individuals with ICE, such as immigration status, it can lead to the unjust targeting of vulnerable populations. This Council should enact new, and strengthen any existing, policies that keep communities’ personal data private. By doing so, New York City can ensure that immigrant communities are not subject to unlawful surveillance or data-sharing practices. For example:

● minimize, as much as possible, the amount of data that is collected and stored by city agencies; ● avoid the retention, transmission, or storing of sensitive data such as immigration status; ● enact transparent policies on data sharing with federal agencies.

New York City’s sanctuary laws are intended to prevent local systems from being used to facilitate federal immigration enforcement. But expansive data collection and surveillance systems built into everyday governance fundamentally weaken that commitment by creating reservoirs of deeply personal information that can be misused, shared, or leaked through system flaws.

The NYPD’s gang database is a striking example of overcollection leading to harm. Oversight bodies, researchers, and community members have long documented that the database overwhelmingly targets Black and Latine youth. The criteria used to justify placement, such as alleged “self-admission” pulled from social media or proximity to others similarly labeled, are unscientific, pretextual, and racially coded. Inclusion in the database does not require a criminal conviction, an arrest, or even reasonable suspicion of criminal activity. Many people included in the list have never been convicted of a crime, others remain in the database long after any alleged conduct.

Yet despite the high level of inaccuracy and discrimination inherent in the database, the consequences of inclusion are immense, particularly for immigrants. The December 2025 report reflected that the NYPD shared gang database information with Homeland Security Investigations through a gang task force, effectively treating the “gang” label as a justification to sidestep sanctuary limitations. In other words, a racially biased and error-prone database became a vehicle for exposing New Yorkers to federal immigration enforcement. While the NYPD has suggested it will “review” access to its systems, limiting access to a flawed database does not solve the underlying problem. The existence of the database itself creates an unjustifiable risk. We have already seen nationally that false gang allegations are used to justify detention and deportation. The city cannot credibly claim it is upholding sanctuary protections while it allows the NYPD to amass inaccurate, unnecessary, and dangerous data about its residents.

These concerns extend beyond just NYPD databases. In correctional settings, the use of digital surveillance technology also raises additional risks of data leaks that could lead to immigration enforcement violations of our city’s sanctuary protections. The jail phone call systems operated by Securus, for example, record and store phone calls and associated biometric and personal data

from incarcerated individuals and their loved ones. Securus not only records jail phone calls, but also stores voiceprints, a form of biometric data, on every individual who uses the system. The city collects biometric data on incarcerated people, as well as anyone who contacts them, whether family members, friends, community groups, or children without proper justification for how the data is being used, who it is shared with, or how long it is stored.

In addition to the invasive collection of biometric data, Securus uses Threads, a platform designed to aggregate and analyze communications and then uses algorithms to track social networks in and outside of prisons, leading to surveillance and guilt by mere association of people in the community. Reporting has indicated that federal agencies, including DHS, previously had access to the data collected by Securus through the federally connected Fusion Center on Riker’s Island.6 Even if the city does not directly provide access to their digital surveillance technology, the collection and storage of this personal data and use of these invasive systems creates a risk that sensitive data may be accessed, repurposed, or disclosed beyond its original purpose because of the commingling of data by third party vendors, or unauthorized agency sharing.

To uphold sanctuary protections, the city must address not only direct and limited cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, but also the underlying data systems that enable it. This requires significantly limiting the collection and use of sensitive information across agencies, eliminating databases such as the NYPD gang database that rely on unverified and discriminatory criteria, and ending the collection and retention of jail phone data (i.e., ending the recording of jail phone calls). These practices generate large volumes of sensitive information that are not necessary for the administration of detention and create substantial risks of misuse, third-party access, and potential disclosure to federal authorities. If city agencies cannot comply with longstanding detainer laws, they cannot be trusted to responsibly manage access to sensitive databases or deploy new and emerging technologies that would further expand information-sharing with federal authorities.

Brooklyn Defender Services supports the passage of the NYC Trust Act (Int. 209-2026), which would strengthen the enforceability of New York City’s existing detainer protections. As described earlier in our testimony, ICE has been able to rely on communication practices at

DOC, information-sharing within Probation, and shifts in executive policy to facilitate civil immigration arrests despite the framework the Council established in 2014. III. The Council must pass the New York City Trust Act (Int. 0209-2026) We urge the Council to support and pass the New York City Trust Act (Int. 0209-2026), which would strengthen accountability when city agencies violate our sanctuary laws. Under this legislation, when an individual’s rights are violated due to local cooperation with federal immigration authorities, they could sue the City for damages. Meaning when agencies unlawfully honor federal detainers or share information with immigration authorities, individuals will have legal recourse. This private right of action is critical because as we have already seen, city agencies such as the NYPD and DOC, have violated these laws, resulting in grave harm to immigrant communities. Allowing individuals to have a private right of action against such illegal behavior could also incentivize the agency to start acting in better faith, for they may be more likely to provide more information as to what is happening due to the fear of a possible future lawsuit. Otherwise, there is no reason for DOC, or any other city agency, to adhere to a law if there are no true repercussions for noncompliance. For this reason, we urge the passage of the New York City Trust Act (Int. 0209-2026), which would create a private right of action so that people wronged by violations of our already existing laws can seek justice in courts. This bill would make sure that city agencies can be held accountable when violations occur, helping ensure compliance with existing laws, and allowing immigrants to feel safer during their legal proceedings. IV. Conclusion We thank the Council for holding an important oversight hearing and for the continued attention to ensure that city agencies comply with our sanctuary laws. Ultimately, the DOI report offers only a narrow glimpse into the broader problem of unlawful cooperation between city agencies and ICE. The actions described in the report are not merely policy failures. They represent outright violations of our laws. Without meaningful transparency and accountability, it is impossible to know the full extent of these practices or how many similar violations have already occurred and are occurring. For this reason we are calling on the Council to pass stronger safeguards. The Council must act to ensure that city agencies comply with the law by passing legislation that closes the communication loopholes between DOC and ICE and by passing the New York City Trust Act (Int. 0209-2026), which would provide a private right of action for individuals harmed by violations of our law. Our client, Byron, was a young man seeking asylum. He was arrested after a fight between him and some other young people. Byron’s defense attorney negotiated a plea that would leave Byron with a Youthful Offender (“YO”) adjudication – importantly, immigration does not consider YO adjudications to meet its definition of “conviction.” The goal of this plea was to preserve Byron’s ability to seek humanitarian relief in the form of asylum and Special Immigrant Juvenile Status. While Byron was at Rikers with pending criminal court proceedings, ICE lodged a detainer against him. Despite the detainer, Byron was eligible for release from Rikers because the Detainer Law specifically exempts YO adjudications from the definition of a “Violent or Serious Crime.” When Byron’s defense attorney reached out to DOC for assurances that Byron would be released, as the law requires , DOC was non-responsive. The defense attorney specifically asked DOC if they were aware that YO adjudications do not count as Violent or Serious Crimes. DOC’s response was merely “we will follow the law.” Relying on that, we advised Byron he was getting out of Rikers, and soon, since he was almost done serving his sentence. Rather than follow the law, DOC turned Byron over to ICE a day before he was to be released. We still don’t know why. Of course , we requested all applicable DOC files, documents, and communications between ICE and DOC, and any determination related to Byron’s eligibility for release. Unsurprisingly, there was nothing in Byron’s DOC file that explained why DOC turned him over to ICE. No judicial warrant. No gang or terrorism related markers. Nothing. Byron’s case exemplifies the need for both transparency and accountability.

First, the whole process was marked by a lack of transparency from DOC. Neither we nor Byron were ever served with the ICE detainer. This is especially problematic because a detainer, as noted on its face, indicates that it should be personally served on the person affected. This left virtually no time for Byron’s attorney to intervene on his behalf and advocate for proper application of the Detainer Law. Unfortunately, this problem is not unique to Byron. We have seen similar cases where DOC failed to indicate whether they planned to turn the clients over to ICE pursuant to a detainer, including when clients were supposed to get released to a treatment program. In one case, they refused to do the calculation in advance until ordered by the J udge who wanted to release the client. Of course we do not have that power. Additionally, in Byron’s case, DOC refused to even engage with us about proper application of the detainer law and completely ignored our proffered legal analysis. When we asked DOC to confirm their awareness that YO adjudications were protected under the detainer law, they told us we can file a FOIL request for their guidance. As you are aware, FOIL requests take months to be processed. Meanwhile, DOC’s release decisions can take hours, hours during which we have no information on what DOC’s interpretation of the detainer law is with respect to our client’s case. Because we suspected DOC might mistakenly consider a YO adjudications to count as Violent or Serious Crimes, we proactively sought to educate them to avoid the egregious result of our client being turned over to ICE due to DOC’s legal error . We would have let Byron’s family know that Byron was not going to make it home that night. We would have made sure he had phone numbers memorized, and let the family know how to track him and how to get in touch with him.
